youtube_title: Could a Rare Bible Beat a Debt Collector in New York? 🦝⚖️
caption: New York's CPLR 5205 lists religious texts used by a debtor's family as exempt without a stated dollar cap, while other books are capped at $500. A textual quirk — not a tested strategy.
script: In New York, you can owe someone a fortune, and they still can't touch your million dollar Bible. [disclaimer] Meet Gary. Gary owes his neighbor Frank a lot of money. Frank sues him. Frank wins. Now Frank is allowed to go after Gary's stuff. He wants the car. He wants the bank account. He even wants the TV. But New York has a list of things a winner is not allowed to take. Regular books? Only about five hundred dollars' worth are safe. But in that same line, the law lists the family Bible. And it gives no dollar limit at all. Wait. So what if Gary's Bible is a super rare antique worth a fortune? Frank reaches for it. Gary just points at the law and smiles. You see, it's like a store where every shelf has a price cap, except one shelf that just says, no limit. Now, nobody has proven this works in court. The book has to really be used by the family. And buying a fancy Bible just to hide money from people you owe can get you in fraud trouble. And there's one more rule. If the money you owe is for the Bible itself, the Bible isn't protected at all. Which is bad news for Gary. Because the money he owes Frank is for the Bible. Only a limited amount. Ordinary books? Up to five hundred dollars' worth. But in that same line, the law separately lists religious texts, family pictures and school books used by the debtor or the family. And for those, it doesn't state a dollar limit.
